Mr. Raghvendra Singh, learned Advocate General assisted by Mrs. Bina Pande,

Mr. Paresh Tripathi, learned Chief Standing Counsel along with Mr. Pradeep

Mr. M.C. Kandpal, learned Senior Counsel assisted by Mr. Chitrarth Kandpal,

 Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
K.M. JOSEPH, C.J. (Oral)
 This bunch of appeals raises common questions and hence we
proceed to pronounce the following common judgment.
2. There is delay in filing some of the appeals. In the
circumstances and reasons narrated in the delay condonation
application and affidavit filed in support thereof and after hearing
learned counsel for the parties, we are of the view that the delay
caused in filing some of the appeals should be condoned.
Accordingly, the delay caused in filing some of the appeals is
condoned and the delay condonation applications are allowed.
3. Heard. Amendment Application filed by the State of Uttar
Pradesh, seeking to add certain grounds, in memo of appeal is not
opposed by the other side, is allowed in Special Appeal No. 1017 of
2017.
4. Appellants are the respondents in the writ petitions. The writ
petitioners are persons, who were working in the Irrigation
Department/Public Works Department. Originally, they were
working as Muster Roll Employees. Subsequently, they were
absorbed in the work-charge establishment. Still later, it is their case
that they have been confirmed. The issue, which is raised in the writ
petitions, appears to be that they are denied pension after including the

15
period they worked as work-charge employees. It is, accordingly, that
they were before this Court in the various writ petitions, which have
led to the present batch of appeals.
5. The writ petitions can be divided into three broad categories in
terms of the reliefs claimed. First being the writ petitions, where there
is a challenge to Article 370 of the Civil Service Regulations
(hereinafter referred to as the "Regulations"). Second batch being the
writ petitions, where there is challenge to Article 370 of the
Regulations and also to the Uttar Pradesh Retirement Benefits Rules,
1961 (hereinafter referred to as the "1961 Rules") to which we shall
advert to in detail. Besides these reliefs, a further relief is claimed for
a direction to pay them pension on the basis that the period of service
under the work-charge establishment would also be counted. Lastly,
in the third category of cases, there is no challenge either to Article
370 of the Regulation or the 1961 Rules, but a direction is sought to
give the writ petitioners the benefit of pension for the period they have
worked as work-charge employees. The learned Single Judge has
proceeded to dispose of the batch of cases in the following fashion:
"50. Accordingly, all the writ petitions are
allowed. Orders, under challenge therein, are quashed
and set aside. Regulation 370(ii) of the Civil Service
Regulations is struck down being ultra vires to Articles
14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The respondents
are directed to count the entire service of the petitioners/
workmen rendered in work-charge capacity followed by
their regularization for the purpose of pensionary and
other retiral benefits including gratuity and thereafter to
release their pension and other retiral benefits including
gratuity within a period of three months from today."
6. It is feeling aggrieved by the same that the State of Uttarakhand
and others are before us. There is also an appeal filed by the State of
Uttar Pradesh i.e. Special Appeal No. 1017 of 2017.
7. We have heard Mr. Raghvendra Singh, learned Advocate
General assisted by Mrs. Bina Pande, learned Standing Counsel for
the State of Uttar Pradesh in the last mentioned appeal. We have also

16
heard Mr. Paresh Tripathi, learned Chief Standing Counsel along with
Mr. Pradeep Joshi and Mr. Anil Kumar Bisht, Standing Counsel, Mr.
Rajeev Singh Bisht and Mr. Narain Dutt, learned Brief Holders in the
appeals filed by the State of Uttarakhand. On behalf of the writ
petitioners, we have heard Mr. M.C. Kandpal, learned Senior Counsel
assisted by Mr. Chitrarth Kandpal, Mr. M.C. Pant, Mr. S.S. Yadav,
Mr. Lalit Belwal, Mr. Amar Shukla, Mr. Harendra Belwal and Mr.
Siddhartha Sah, learned counsel.
Arguments on behalf of the learned Advocate General for the
State of Uttar Pradesh
8. The learned Advocate General for the State of Uttar Pradesh
would first of all point out from the cause title of the writ petition that
there is only one petitioner in the writ petition. He would further draw
our attention to the body of the writ petition and point out that the writ
petitioner has referred to a list of persons. He would complain that
there is no authorization for the writ petitioner to file the writ petition
on behalf of all the persons, who are referred to. He would submit
that the writ petitioner is not a registered Association and, therefore,
he questions the locus standi of the writ petitioner to represent the
various persons mentioned in the writ petition. Moving on, he would
submit that this is a case where the matter is governed specifically by
the Rules, which have been made under Article 309 of the
Constitution of India, which are called the Uttar Pradesh Retirement
Benefits Rules, 1961. He would submit that it is these 1961 Rules,
which confers the right to pension. It is pointed out that in Rule 3(8)
of the 1961 Rules "Qualifying Service" has been defined as follows:
 "3. In these rules unless there is anything
repugnant in the subject or context-
 (8) "Qualifying service" means service which
qualifies for pension in accordance with the provisions of
Article 368 of the Civil Service Regulations:

Provided that continuous temporary or officiating
service under the Government of Uttar Pradesh followed

17
without interruption by confirmation in the same or any
other post except-
(i) periods of temporary or officiating service in
a non-pensionable establishment,
(ii) periods of service in a work-charged
establishment, and
(iii) periods of service in a post paid from
contingencies, shall also count as qualifying
service.
Note :- If service is rendered in a non-pensionable
establishment, work-charged establishment or in a
post paid from contingencies falls between two
period of temporary service in a pensionable
establishment or between a period of temporary
service and permanent service in a pensionable
establishment, it will not constitute an interruption
of service."
9. Rule 4 of the 1961 Rules, contemplates the amount of
superannuation, retiring, invalid and compensation pension or gratuity
shall be the appropriate amount set out in the Annexure. Therefore,
with reference to Rule 3(8)(ii), the period of service in a work-charge
establishment stand excludes for the purpose of calculating the
pensionary benefits. He would submit that conspicuous by its absence
in the writ petition is a challenge to the 1961 Rules. He would
contend that unless the Rules are successfully challenged, no
mandamus will lie to grant pension, as has been done by the learned
Single Judge. He would point out that the employees working in a
work-charge establishment form a separate class. In this regard, he
drew our attention to the judgments in the following cases:
i. Jaswant Singh and others Vs. Union of India and
 others reported in (1979) 4 SCC 440.
ii. State of Rajasthan Vs. Kunji Ram reported in (1997) 2
 SCC 517.
iii. State Electricity Board and others Vs. Jagjiwan Ram
 and others reported in (2009) 3 SCC 661.

10. Learned Advocate General for the State of Uttar Pradesh also
drew our attention to the judgment in the case of Jai Prakash Vs.
State of U.P. & 4 others reported in 2014 (2) ADJ 169. He would

18
point out from page no. 111 of the compilation, which he has made
available, that the Special Leave Petition filed against the same came
to be dismissed. He would also further draw our attention to a recent
order of the Hon'ble Apex Court by which the Hon'ble Apex Court
has issued notice in a matter arising from judgment of Allahabad High
Court dated 03.02.2017 in relation to challenge to the 1961 Rules and
Regulation 370 of the Civil Service Regulations. He would further
submit that in the writ petition, conspicuous by its absence is details
as to the writ petitioners. He expands his argument by contending that
having regard to the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case
of State of Uttarakhand and another Vs. Umakant Joshi reported
in 2012 (1) U.D. 583, if the relief is to be granted in respect of a cause
of action, which arose prior to 09.11.2000, which is the appointed day
under the U.P. States Reorganisation Act, 2000, this Court may not
have the jurisdiction. He would further point out that the judgment of
the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the case of Kesar Chand Vs.
State of Punjab and others reported in AIR 1988 Punjab &
Haryana 265 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Punjab's case), which
had struck down Clause 3.17, cannot apply to the State of Uttar
Pradesh, particularly, bearing in mind the fact that even the 1961
Rules have not been called in question. He would further contend that
the judgment of the learned Single Judge may not bear scrutiny by this
Court. He would contend that the learned Single Judge has also
adverted to the deletion of Articles 668, 669 and 670 and came to the
conclusion that upon deletion of these regulations in the Civil Service
Regulations, the consequence would be that the employee concerned
would become regular. Learned Advocate General for the State of
Uttar Pradesh would impugn this finding. He would submit that the
mere deletion of these provisions would not have the result of their
being becoming deemed regular employees; on the other hand, these
deletions would have only prospective operation. In fact, he would
point out that many of the writ petitioners were confirmed much prior
to the deletion of these provisions, which took place in the year 2000.

19
He would further impugn the finding of the learned Single Judge that
with the deletion of the provisions in question, Article 370 would
become otiose. His contention is that even after deletion of these
provisions, the existing work-charge employees would continue as
such. The effect of deletion would only be that there would be no
fresh appointments as work-charge. He would contend that by
deletion, Article 370 has not been rendered otiose. In fact, the
deletion has no effect in regard to many of the employees. He would
further complain that the learned Single Judge has, in striking down
Article 370, not given any reasoning as would suffice in law to sustain
the finding. The legislative instrument to be afflicted with the vice,
which is frowned upon under Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of
India, must be one, which is afflicted with such inequality that it treats
two equals as unequals or unequals as equals. In this case, on the
other hand, persons working in the work-charge establishment are
distinct from the persons, who are having regular appointments. He
expatiates and submits that such persons do not work as against any
post. Without working as against any post, he questions their right to
be treated alike with persons, who are regularly appointed. The
purport of Article 370 is to exclude, according to him, persons, who
are working in the work-charge establishment, for reasons, which can
easily be perceived and as is clear from a catena of decisions, which is
referred to by the Hon'ble Apex Court. He calls in question the
judgment of the Punjab & Haryana High Court and would submit that
it may not hold good after the judgments, which he has adverted to
and which, we have referred to, delineating the actual scope of work,
which is done and the status of the work-charge employees. As far as
the decision in the case of Habib Khan Vs. State of Uttarakhand
and others (hereinafter referred to as the "Habib Khan's case") to
which we shall advert to, in detail, his answer is that the State of Uttar
Pradesh is not a party in the said judgment. He would submit that the
duty of the Court is to decipher the ratio decidendi in a case, as it is
only a ratio decidendi, which is law under Article 141 of the

20
Constitution of India, which is binding on the High Courts.
Observations, which are made by the Court, which do not amount to
the ratio decidendi can be ignored by the Court. In this regard, when
attention was drawn to the judgment in the case of Ram Deo Tiwari
Vs. The State of U.P. & Ors. (hereinafter referred to as the "Tiwari's
case"), he would contend that there is no law, as such, which is laid
down. He would submit that the judgment did not proceed on
consideration of any legal issue and would also rely, at any rate, on
the subsequent order passed by the Hon'ble Apex Court, by which
notice has been issued in regard to the validity of the 1961 Rules and
Regulation 370 of Civil Service Regulations. According to him, all
that happened in this case is that the writ petitioners were persons,
who were engaged in the work-charge establishment. By the very
connotation of work-charge establishment, employees engaged in the
work-charge establishments are ordinarily to be retrenched after the
work is executed, but the State used to continue them out of a sense of
fairness and thus it is that they continued for long period of time
before they were finally confirmed. Therefore, such service, which
they have rendered cannot enure for the calculation of pensionary
benefits.
11. The learned Advocate General for the State of Uttar Pradesh
also relied on the judgment of the Division Bench of the Allahabad
High Court in the case of Krishna Kumar &27 Ors. Vs. State of
U.P. Thru. Prin. Secy. Lok Nirman Vibhag & 5 Ors. (Misc. Bench
No. 20486 of 2016). Therein, after an exhaustive consideration the
Division Bench has taken the view that in the light of the judgment of
the Hon'ble Apex Court explaining the actual nature of the
employment of a work-charge employee, there is no valid reason for
striking down provision contained in Article 370. It is the argument
of the learned Advocate General that the matter is pending before the
Hon'ble Apex Court and notice has been issued

21
Contentions on behalf of learned Chief Standing Counsel for the
State of Uttarakhand.
12. Mr. Paresh Tripathi, learned Chief Standing Counsel appearing
on behalf of the State of Uttarakhand/appellants in the appeals filed by
the State of Uttarakhand would address the following submissions
before us:
 He would, first of all, draw our attention to the judgment of the
Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Punjab State Electricity Board
and another Vs. Narata Singh and another reported in (2010) 4
SCC 317 (hereinafter referred to as the "Narata Singh's case"). This
is a judgment in which the judgment of the Punjab & Haryana High
Court declaring the corresponding provision in the State of Punjab
was declared invalid came to be followed. Reference to this judgment
is made only to contend that this judgment will only hold good qua
the employees in the State of Punjab. A Rule, which is made by the
law-giver, unless it is to have operation beyond the borders of the
State, as it would be in the case of a Central Legislation, would be
confined to the said State only. Therefore, he would submit that the
said judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court cannot be
stressed upon. Next, he would submit that the judgment, which is
relied on by the writ petitioners to which also we shall make
advertence in greater detail, namely, the decision in Habib Khan's
case, which arose from this Court, is only a judgment in personam; it
is not a judgment in rem. The Court has only directed to grant the
benefits to the parties in the said Appeal. He would emphatically
submit that no law, as such, has been laid down in Habib Khan's case.
He would contend that the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court did
not consider that the persons, who are absorbed in the work-charge
establishment, were so absorbed without any selection and they
cannot be likened to the persons, who have joined after undergoing a
proper selection. He would submit that the result of making available
the pensionary benefits to those for the period they have worked as
work-charge employees would result in the creation of unequals being

22
treated equally. On the one hand, there are persons, who have put in
regular service after undergoing proper selection and their service is
counted and they get pension on the said basis, whereas if persons,
who have not undergone selection and their period in the work-charge
establishment is directed to be taken into consideration, this would
amount to treating unequals equally. It is further contended that the
learned Single Judge has erred in finding that the employees were
paid from out of the Salary Head; they were actually only paid either
from the Labour Head or from the Contingency Fund. He further
submits that the 1961 Rules have not been challenged. The 1961
Rules have the effect of overriding the Regulations. Till they are
regularized (apparently confirmed), they are not employees; they
cannot claim benefit of seniority. He also would adopt this line of
argument of the learned Advocate General for the State of Uttar
Pradesh, namely, the effect of deletion of the various Articles is not
that they would become regular merely on deletion of some Articles.
He drew our attention to the Government Order dated 25.10.2005.
According to him, those persons, who have been confirmed after the
date of the said Government Order, would be treated as new entrants
and they would be covered by the Pension Scheme, which has been
enunciated under the said Government Order. Therefore, there cannot
be any question of claiming the pensionary benefits for the period
anterior to their service being regularized. He also attempted to
question the reasoning of the judgment of the Punjab & Haryana High
Court. Mr. Paresh Tripathi, learned Chief Standing Counsel would
also contend that the Habib Khan's case does not contain the ratio
decidendi, as no reason or logic is considered in the light of non-challenge to the 1961 Rules. Appellants also have a case that huge
financial commitments would be incurred running into thousands of
crore if the State is to be saddled with the liability, which would arise
from the judgment of the learned Single Judge.
Learned Chief Standing Counsel in the course of his arguments
(though no ground is taken in the counter affidavits) would contend

23
that these are the cases where there is no confirmation but only
regularization and it is submitted that in the appeal it is stated.
According to Mr. M.C. Pant, learned counsel for the writ petitioners,
granting of permanent status after regularization is merely a
ministerial act.
13. Per contra, Mr. M.C. Kandpal, learned senior counsel appearing
on behalf of the writ petitioners in two appeals would submit that
there is discrimination being practiced. He would submit that the writ
petitions have been filed by persons whose petitions were allowed by
this Court both at the level of the learned Single Judge and also at the
level of the Division Bench and Special Leave Petitions have been
dismissed; and those orders have become final. He would submit that
some persons in the Irrigation Department/Public Works Department
are being paid on the basis of the said orders and still further he would
point out the decision in Habib Khan's case. He would submit that
this discrimination cannot be allowed to continue. Therefore, he
would pray for dismissal of the writ petitions; otherwise, he adopts the

 "9. We have considered the respective submissions.
Generally speaking, a work charged establishment is an
establishment of which the expenses are chargeable to works.
The pay and allowances of the employees who are engaged on a
work charged establishment are usually shown under a
specified sub-head of the estimated cost of works. The work
charged employees are engaged for execution of a specified
work or project and their engagement comes to an end on
completion of the work or project. The source and mode of
engagement/recruitment of work charged employees, their pay
and conditions of employment are altogether different from the
persons appointed in the regular establishment against
sanctioned posts after following the procedure prescribed under
the relevant Act or rules and their duties and responsibilities are
also substantially different than those of regular employees.

under the Industrial Disputes Act or the rights flowing from any
particular statute but they cannot be treated at par with the
employees of regular establishment. They can neither claim
regularization of service as of right nor they can claim pay
scales and other financial benefits at par with regular
employees. If the service of a work charged employee is
regularized under any statute or a scheme framed by the
employer, then he becomes member of regular establishment
from the date of regularization. His service in the work charged
establishment cannot be clubbed with service in a regular
establishment unless a specific provision to that effect is made

either in the relevant statute or the scheme of regularization. In
other words, if the statute or scheme under which service of
work charged employee is regularized does not provide for
counting of past service, the work charged employee cannot
claim benefit of such service for the purpose of fixation of
seniority in the regular cadre, promotion to the higher posts,
fixation of pay in the higher scales, grant of increments etc.
 11. In Jaswant Singh and others vs. Union of India and
others [(1979) 4 SCC 440], this Court considered the issue
relating to nature of work charged establishment, status of work
charged employees and held that the employees appointed on
work charged establishment are not entitled to service benefits

establishments and the persons employed on those

framed for the persons engaged in the work-charged
